summary: Specifies the architecture, behavior, textual representation, and usage of IPv6 addresses of different scopes. It intentionally avoids the syntax and usage of unicast site-local addresses, per an IPv6 working group decision.

plainLanguage.summary: Some IPv6 addresses only make sense within one part of a network, and the same address can appear in separate parts. This RFC explains how a computer identifies the right zone when sending or interpreting such an address.

questions: what is an ipv6 scope zone
what does the percent sign mean in an ipv6 address
what is a link-local address zone id
how do ipv6 zone indices work
subtitle: How IPv6 identifies the network zone for an address that is not globally unique.

tldr.problem: A non-global IPv6 address can be reused in separate parts of a network. A node connected to several such zones needs to know which zone an address belongs to.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines scope zones and node-local zone indices, then gives rules for packet handling and a textual address form that adds a percent sign and zone identifier.
tldr.outcome: It defines an architecture for link-local and multicast scopes while intentionally excluding unicast site-local addresses. RFC 4007 was updated by RFC 7346 and RFC 9844.

today: RFC 4007 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7346 and RFC 9844. Read those documents with its scoped-address architecture.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Needs Scoped Address Rules
sections.content:
Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) includes global and non-global addresses. A link-local address, for example, identifies an interface on one link, not throughout the Internet. This RFC describes the architecture, behavior, textual form, and use of addresses with different scopes.

The document focuses on link-local and multicast scopes. It intentionally leaves out unicast site-local addresses because the IPv6 working group decided to deprecate their syntax and use.
sections.plainLanguage: A link-local address is meaningful on one link, so it may also appear on another link. The RFC defines how a node keeps those uses separate.

sections.title: Address Scopes and Scope Zones
sections.content:
An address's scope is the topological span in which it can identify an interface. Unicast addresses discussed here have link-local or global scope; multicast addresses have fourteen possible scopes, from interface-local through global. The loopback address ::1 is treated as link-local on an imaginary loopback link.

A zone is one connected region with a given scope. Scope describes the size of a region; a zone is a particular instance of that region. The zone is not encoded in a non-global address, so two links can each use fe80::1.

Zones of the same scope do not overlap, smaller zones fit inside larger ones, and packets between interfaces in one zone are not routed outside it. Each interface belongs to one zone of each scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Scope describes how far an address is meant to reach; a zone is one specific region at that scope. The address alone may not identify which region is meant.

sections.title: Zone Indices Are Local to a Node
sections.content:
A node assigns a distinct zone index to each zone of a scope that it touches. The node uses the index internally to distinguish repeated non-global addresses. These indices are local to the node; the other end of a link can use different values.

The RFC says an implementation should support a default zone for each scope and should reserve index 0 for that default. At the time of the RFC, nodes could not discover automatically which interfaces shared a zone, so implementations needed a way to configure zone indices manually.

By default, an implementation should assign a unique interface index and a unique link index to each interface. Configuration may be needed when interfaces share a link or when zones of larger multicast scopes are involved.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node keeps its own zone labels. A label identifies a zone only inside that node, so the same label can mean something different on another node.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving, and Forwarding
sections.content:
When an application sends to a non-global, non-loopback address, it needs a way to tell IPv6 which zone it means. On receipt, the arrival interface identifies the zone for a non-global source or destination address; the RFC recommends passing the relevant zone indices to the upper layer.

A router chooses a route using the destination's zone. It then checks whether the selected outgoing interface would take the packet outside the source address's zone. If so, it discards the packet and, for a unicast destination, sends an Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6 (ICMPv6) Destination Unreachable message with Code 2, “beyond scope of source address.”

A node processing a Routing Header must discard a packet if the next address has a smaller scope than the original destination. Otherwise it continues forwarding under the same zone rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending application identifies the intended zone, and the arrival interface helps identify a zone for received addresses. A router drops a packet if forwarding it would carry a scoped source address outside its zone.

sections.title: Keeping Multicast Routing Information Inside Zones
sections.content:
The routing discussion concerns multicast scopes. A routing protocol at a zone boundary must maintain connectivity within each zone and protect the integrity of information between zones.

A router should keep a forwarding view for global groups and for scoped groups in each attached zone. When it sends routing information through an interface, it must not include information about other zones. The RFC illustrates this with a router connected to three organizations: organization-specific group information is shared only among interfaces in that organization.
sections.plainLanguage: A router at a zone boundary must keep each zone connected without leaking its scoped multicast routing information to other zones.

sections.title: Writing an Address with a Zone Identifier
sections.content:
For a non-global address, an implementation should support the textual form <address>%<zone_id>. The percent sign separates the IPv6 address from a string that identifies its zone. The form applies to non-global unicast and multicast addresses, but is not intended for global, loopback, or unspecified addresses.

The zone identifier can be a non-negative decimal index, or an implementation may support another string such as an interface name. When the default zone is intended, the percent sign and zone identifier may be omitted. The RFC gives fe80::2%3 as an example for selecting link index 3.

This notation is for use within one node. It must not be sent over the network unless every node interpreting it agrees on the meaning. The RFC does not define how to combine the notation with a literal IPv6 address in a URL.
sections.plainLanguage: Add a percent sign and a zone label when a non-global IPv6 address needs clarification. The label is local to the computer and is not normally part of a network packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A limited-scope address without a zone index cannot be used safely in some security contexts. The RFC gives examples involving IKE traffic selectors and access-control lists that need to distinguish among zones.

Routers should keep zone-specific multicast routing information inside its zone. The textual notation is restricted to one node, but a malicious node could send a textual address with a zone index as data to mislead a receiver; implementations should treat such data carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: Security rules that use a scoped address need enough information to identify its zone. A computer should also treat zone labels received as ordinary data with care.
